title: Toyota Production System
author: Taiichi Ohno
theme: A factory becomes efficient not by producing more, but by relentlessly removing waste so that only what is needed is made, when it is needed.
summary: Taiichi Ohno, the engineer who built Toyota's manufacturing approach, explains in this short book how and why it came about. Post-war Japan could not copy American mass production. Demand was small, customers wanted many different models, and money and space were scarce. Toyota had to find a way to make cars cheaply in low volumes, and Ohno's answer was to attack waste wherever it appeared.

The system rests on two pillars. The first is just-in-time: each process makes only the parts the next process needs, in the quantity needed, at the moment needed. To make this work, Ohno turned the usual flow around. Instead of earlier stages pushing parts forward, later stages go back and take what they have used, much as shoppers take goods from a supermarket shelf that is then restocked. Simple cards called kanban carry the instructions for what to withdraw and what to produce.

The second pillar is autonomation, or automation with a human touch. Machines are built to stop by themselves when something goes wrong, and workers are expected to halt the line when they spot a problem. Stopping feels costly, but it prevents defects from multiplying and forces the cause to be fixed.

Ohno lists several kinds of waste, including waiting, unnecessary movement, transport, excess processing, defects and surplus inventory. He treats overproduction as the worst, because making too much early hides every other problem under piles of stock.
He also urges smoothing production so that volume and mix stay level, cutting changeover times so small batches become practical, and asking why repeatedly until the real cause of a problem is found.
Throughout, Ohno stresses that the system is a way of thinking rather than a set of tools. Its aim is lower cost through honest attention to how work actually flows.
takeaway: Make only what is needed when it is needed, stop to fix problems at once, and treat overproduction as the waste that hides all the others.

questions.q: Why could Toyota not simply copy American mass production after the war?
options: Demand was low, model variety was high, and capital was scarce
American firms refused to share their methods
questions.why: Mass production depends on huge volumes of few models, which did not fit Japan's small and varied market.

questions.q: What are the two pillars of the Toyota Production System?
questions.why: Ohno describes just-in-time flow and machines or workers that stop on abnormalities as the system's foundations.

questions.q: Which form of waste does Ohno regard as the most harmful?
questions.why: Making too much too early creates stock that conceals every other problem in the process.

questions.q: In a just-in-time system, how do parts move between processes?
options: Earlier processes push as much as they can make
A central planner ships parts to every station weekly
Later processes withdraw only what they have used from earlier ones
questions.why: Ohno reversed the flow so that downstream use pulls production from upstream.

questions.q: What gave Ohno the idea for the pull system?
options: The way American supermarkets restock shelves after customers take goods
questions.why: A supermarket refills only what shoppers remove, which became the model for withdrawing and replacing parts.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a kanban card?
options: To advertise the product to customers
To carry instructions on what to withdraw and what to produce
questions.why: Kanban is the information tool that tells each process what to take and what to make.

questions.q: What does 'automation with a human touch' mean in practice?
options: Letting machines run without supervision at all times
Paying workers according to machine output
Building machines that stop themselves when something goes wrong
questions.why: Autonomation means equipment detects abnormalities and halts, so defects are not mass-produced.

questions.q: Why are workers encouraged to stop the line when they see a problem?
options: So that defects do not multiply and the root cause gets fixed
To slow output and raise prices
questions.why: A short stop now prevents many faulty products later and forces the problem into the open.

questions.q: Why does Ohno stress reducing changeover times?
options: It makes small-batch production of varied models practical
It allows longer runs of a single model
It removes the need for any inventory planning
It lets the plant close earlier each day
questions.why: Quick changeovers remove the cost penalty of switching models, enabling small lots and level production.

questions.q: What is the purpose of repeatedly asking 'why' about a problem?
options: To reach the underlying cause instead of the visible symptom
questions.why: Asking why several times digs beneath surface symptoms until the true root cause is identified.
